newsitem.title: INDIA: Low prices drive down Indian sugar exports.
newsitem.headline: Low prices drive down Indian sugar exports.

text.p: India's sugar exports in the 1996/97 (October-September) season had dropped to a trickle due to low world prices, a dip in domestic output and government's decision to end trade controls, officials said on Wednesday.

"International sugar prices are so low that our prices are not competitive in the market," said a senior official of the state-owned Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA).
The official told Reuters that export inquiries too were not very encouraging.

APEDA which was authorised by the Food Ministry to export 250,000 tonnes of sugar in the season after deregulation, had so far issued licences for the export of about 210,000 tonnes but physical exports were much lower, the official said.
"Only 50,000 tonnes have been physically exported, 90 percent of it to Pakistan by rail," he said.
He said small quantities had been shipped to Singapore, Maldives and Canada.
In January the government ended the Indian Sugar and General Industry Export-Import Corp's (ISGIEC) monopoly over sugar exports. ISGIEC is a private corporation set up by the sugar milling industry.

The decision was considered an important step towards freeing the sugar industry from a decades-old system of licensing, pricing and distribution geared to balance the interests of producers and consumers.
But S.L. Jain secretary general of the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA) criticised the government for the fall in exports.
Jain said prior to January, ISGIEC undertook sugar exports and any loss on exports were shared on a pro rata basis by its members.
The provision for loss-sharing in the Sugar Export Promotion Act, 1958 became redundant after the government decided to issue an ordinance to repeal the act.
"If this policy was not there, exports could be taking place and the losses would be shared by the industry," Jain said.
Jain said international prices have normally been lower than Indian prices but Indian sugar exports had been doing well.
Industry officials said Indian sugar for export was quoted at $370 per tonne compared with $330 for sugar of similar quality from other countries.
India had exported about 1.1 million tonnes until December 1996 when the government deregulated sugar exports, Food Ministry officials said.
Vimal Jain, a industry official, said India's sugar output in the 1996/97 season was expected to dip sharply to about 12.8 million tonnes from the previous year's record 16.45 million.
He said there was no fear of shortage since India held plenty of carryover sugar stocks.
As on June 15 this year India held 10.4 million tonnes of sugar stocks compared with 11.0 million a year ago, Jain said.
India annually consumes about 14 million tonnes of sugar.
ISMA's Jain said sugarcane growers had shifted to crops like cotton, oilseeds, plantation and short gestation crops leading to a drop in output.
He said it was too early to predict output in the 1997/98 season.
